structure.title: Chapters 1–5 · Sort the arts by what they do
structure.text: Aristotle starts with differences a spectator can recognise. People represent actions through rhythm, words or melody, and a performer may tell a story or act it out. Those distinctions prepare the comparison of tragedy with epic.

structure.title: Chapters 6–18 · Build an action that holds together
structure.text: Once tragedy has been divided into parts, plot gets the hardest questions. Which incident has to happen here? What kind of discovery makes earlier action suddenly look different? Aristotle writes as someone who expects the poet to try another arrangement and see what breaks.

structure.title: Chapters 19–26 · Words, epic and hard cases
structure.text: Attention moves to diction and the larger compass of epic, then to objections a critic might raise about an impossibility or inconsistency. Aristotle asks what a work is trying to achieve before deciding whether a departure counts as a fault.

people.name: Plot
people.text: A string of adventures can all happen to the same hero and still lack unity. Aristotle looks for a connection strong enough that taking a piece away alters what the remaining events amount to.

people.name: Recognition and reversal
people.role: Two ways a scene can turn
people.text: News meant to reassure someone can disclose the very thing they dread. The change in knowledge can reverse the direction of the action in the same stroke, giving the poet two effects with one arrival.

context.title: Examples from Greek plays
context.text: Aristotle often names a play as briefly as one might name a familiar film. Where the title is unfamiliar, the detail he selects usually tells you what the example needs to demonstrate, such as a discovery arising from the events themselves.

notice.why: When an episode can be moved or cut with no effect on its neighbours, the loss reveals something about the original design. Unity here can be examined by an editor with scissors.

notice.text: Notice what a spectator could feel with eyes shut.
notice.why: A spectacular sight can shock. Aristotle prizes the poet who arranges events so that simply hearing what happened produces pity and fear, locating part of the achievement before the actors take the stage.

opening: A messenger arrives with good news, and the news destroys the person it was meant to comfort. Aristotle is interested in how a story can produce a reversal like that without feeling contrived. He studies what makes events belong together, why recognition can hurt, and how an invented action can arouse real pity and fear. His surviving account is compact enough to read quickly, but it keeps returning attention to the difficult craft beneath a story that seems to unfold inevitably.
